title: Who Pays What
objective: After this level you can compare tax systems where the rate rises with income to systems with one rate.
summary: Progressive taxes take a bigger share of bigger incomes, flat taxes the same share, regressive taxes a smaller share. Brackets tax only the extra dollars, so a raise never cuts your pay.

cards.headline: Could a raise push you into a higher tax bracket and leave you poorer?
cards.body: No. Only the extra dollars pay the higher rate, so your take-home pay still rises. Why that's true opens up the bigger question of this level: how should a tax bill be shared out?

cards.headline: Three ways to share the bill
cards.body: Picture three people earning very different incomes. A progressive tax takes a bigger share from the higher incomes; the US federal income tax works this way. A proportional, or flat, tax takes the same share from everyone, like the US Medicare payroll tax. A regressive tax takes a smaller share as income rises. In 1994, Estonia became the first country in Eastern Europe to swap its income tax for a flat one.

cards.headline: Brackets are buckets
cards.body: Progressive income taxes usually work in brackets. Picture your income pouring into a row of buckets. The first bucket is taxed at the lowest rate; only the money that spills into the next bucket pays the next rate, and so on. So when a raise tips you into a higher bracket, only the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate. Your take-home pay goes up. Always.
cards.callout: A higher bracket taxes the extra dollars, not all of them.

mascot.line: A stubborn myth: a raise can shrink your take-home pay. It can't; only the extra dollars pay more.

cards.headline: The same rate, a different bite
cards.body: Remember Level 51's taxes on what you buy? A sales tax charges everyone the same rate at the till. But lower-income households spend a bigger share of their income on goods, while higher-income households spend a smaller share of theirs. So measured against income, a sales tax takes a bigger bite from lower incomes. That makes it regressive, even though the rate never changes.

cards.headline: One rate or rising rates? Both sides of the argument

items.label: For a flat income tax
points: Simpler: many people could file their own return
Clears out deductions special interests exploit
Lower top rates encourage working, saving and investing

items.label: Against a flat income tax
points: Less fair: shifts the burden toward lower and middle incomes

cards.headline: Who pays: explained
learned: Progressive: bigger incomes pay a bigger share
Flat: the same share for everyone
Regressive: bigger incomes pay a smaller share
Brackets tax only the extra dollars

questions.prompt: In a progressive tax, how does the share of income paid change as income rises?

options.label: It stays exactly the same
options.rationale: That's a proportional, or flat, tax.

options.label: It drops to zero above a set income
options.rationale: No: the share rises with income.

questions.explanation: A progressive tax, like the US federal income tax, takes a bigger share of higher incomes.

questions.prompt: Mia's raise moves part of her income into a higher tax bracket. What happens to her pay after tax?

options.label: It falls, because all her income is now taxed at the higher rate
options.rationale: Only the dollars inside the higher bracket pay that rate.

options.label: It stays the same, because the extra tax cancels the raise
options.rationale: The higher rate applies only to the extra dollars, so she keeps part of them.

options.label: It rises, because only the extra dollars pay the higher rate
It rises by the full raise, because raises are tax-free
options.rationale: The extra dollars are taxed, just at the higher rate.

questions.explanation: Brackets work like buckets: only the income that spills into the higher bracket pays the higher rate.

questions.prompt: From Level 51: a sales tax charges everyone the same rate. Why is it still called regressive?

options.label: Rich shoppers get a discount at the till
options.rationale: Everyone pays the same rate at the till.

options.label: It is only charged in poorer neighborhoods
options.rationale: It applies everywhere the tax is set.

options.label: Its rate falls as prices rise
options.rationale: The rate stays the same; what differs is the share of income spent.

options.label: Lower-income households spend a bigger share of their income

questions.explanation: Measured against income, the same sales tax takes a bigger bite from households that spend more of what they earn.
